summary: The article explains how fiscal reform can advance sustainable development through green taxation, public investment, new success metrics beyond GDP, and international tax coordination. It cites dated examples from Sweden, Brazil, the European Parliament, UNCTAD and the US Treasury. It also notes political obstacles from vested interests and argues that sustainability and fiscal health reinforce each other.
one_line: Fiscal policy reforms such as green taxes, sustainable public spending, and global tax coordination can drive sustainable development despite political obstacles.
key_facts: On November 15, 2023, economist Dr. Samantha Higgins said at the Global Economic Forum in New York, "It's no longer just about balancing the books."
On September 10, 2023, Sweden announced a tax overhaul raising taxes on fossil fuels while decreasing income taxes.
Swedish Finance Minister Lars Magnusson said the Swedish tax move aimed to "steer our economy towards a greener future without placing undue burden on our citizens."
Many governments offer tax credits for renewable energy projects, electric vehicle adoption, and energy-efficient home upgrades.
On December 12, 2023, Brazil unveiled a plan to redirect part of its public expenditure to preserving the Amazon rainforest.

On September 21, 2023, Spanish social economist Lucia Fernandez introduced 'Sustainable Development Scorecards' in the European Parliament to assess fiscal policies on environmental goals, inequality and quality of life.
Traditional metrics like GDP growth are criticized for not capturing the health of a society or ecosystem.
International coordination can prevent a 'race to the bottom' where countries compete with lower taxes and lax environmental regulations.
On January 24, 2024, the UN Conference on Trade and Development in Geneva facilitated an agreement to harmonize tax policies, including a global minimum corporate tax rate.
On February 20, 2024, US Treasury Secretary Michael DaSilva told Congress that reform requires political will, transparent policy-making and public engagement.
Incumbent industries and vested interests can oppose reforms that reduce their profitability.
Investments in renewable energy can reduce reliance on imported fuels, improve trade balances and lessen exposure to volatile fossil fuel markets.
